claims.text: Pristine Q235 steel has a naturally occurring ultrathin surface oxide film.
The formation kinetics and microstructure of the oxide film on Q235 steel are temperature-dependent.
At room temperature, the oxide film on Q235 steel develops slowly into a continuous protective layer.
A dense or compact oxide layer can act as a barrier that improves oxidation or corrosion resistance.
Elevated temperature accelerates oxide formation on Q235 steel.
Faster oxide formation at elevated temperature produces a thinner film on Q235 steel.
Elevated-temperature exposure produces a more porous, non-uniform, and defective oxide film than room-temperature exposure.
A porous and defective oxide film permits aggressive chloride ions to penetrate to the metal-film interface.
Penetration of aggressive ions through the defective film triggers corrosion processes.
Q235 steel exposed at 80°C in 3.5 wt.% NaCl will have a higher corrosion rate than Q235 steel exposed at approximately 25°C under otherwise identical conditions.
The elevated-temperature samples will exhibit higher corrosion current densities than the room-temperature reference.
The elevated-temperature samples will exhibit greater weight loss than the room-temperature reference.
The elevated-temperature samples will exhibit more negative corrosion potentials, which are presented as an indicator of a higher corrosion rate.
Surface analysis will reveal a more porous and discontinuous oxide morphology after elevated-temperature exposure.
Minor variations in steel composition and experimental setup may change the quantitative film-thickness and corrosion-rate differences.
Secondary microstructural factors not captured by surface oxide analysis may influence corrosion behavior.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the room-temperature comparator an 'untreated' reference, but the baseline explicitly exposes that comparator to the corrosive medium. Only the pre-exposure samples are untreated.
